source.title: AlphaZero Neural Scaling and Zipf's Law: a Tale of Board Games and Power Laws

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some equations and formatting are flattened, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines scaling in AlphaZero and reports inverse scaling in Oware and Checkers, plus state-specific loss trends that qualify whether scaling behavior transfers to an RL setting. Its measurements differ from language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure language-model loss, training-token scaling, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Its loss analyses use AlphaZero value loss, often against game-state rank or state subsets, rather than a fitted loss-versus-resource power law. Rows for rank- and training-stage-based loss results are retained as related findings but are not treated as tests of the listed versions. The text also discusses cited scaling results; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures how AlphaZero playing strength scales with network size in four board games, so it bears on V5 (power-law scaling in another training regime). It reports that Elo scaling in Oware and Checkers abruptly reverses beyond a size threshold. It also reports that the Connect Four size-scaling exponent shifts with inference temperature. It does not measure language-model loss, extrapolation, compute-optimal splits or architecture shape, so V1–V4, V6 and V7 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim that inference temperature causally shifts the Connect Four size-scaling exponent along with the Zipf exponent, nonlinearly. They propose that inverse scaling arises because large models forget early-game states under target non-stationarity (dormant neurons), while late-game states with fixed labels are retained.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses AlphaZero self-play and game-value loss/Elo, rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy and parameter/token/compute sweeps. It examines loss by state rank and state subset, and reports inverse Elo scaling.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary by game and state subset: Oware early-game loss worsens with model size while late-game loss improves. Inference temperature changes the Connect Four state-frequency curve and size-scaling exponent, although the paper says the exponent correlation is nonlinear.

fits_no_version.finding: In Oware, larger agents have worse value loss on early-game states and better loss on late-game states. The largest agent's early-game loss worsens late in training while its late-game loss keeps improving.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In AlphaZero, extra capacity can shift fitting toward frequent, trivial late-game states at the expense of important early-game states, coinciding with inverse scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Connect Four value loss rises with state-frequency rank even though higher-rank states are easier to solve. Larger agents have lower loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AlphaZero agents optimize state loss in descending order of frequency, consistent with the quantization model.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 (39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
record.problems: The paper says game states are only proxies for independent task quanta, and many unique states occurring once are omitted from its main state-frequency analyses. Checkers' late-game frequency anomaly is difficult to visualize. The authors also state that loss is only a proxy for performance and that the relation between loss and multi-agent Elo is non-trivial. Relevant loss-versus-size findings are mainly qualitative; exact values and fitted exponents are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant outcomes were left out. Results about Zipf curves, temperature, and state-rank loss that do not measure a listed version are summarized under gate_note or fits_no_version rather than entered as version rows.

untested.parts: No extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation measured; the RL compute-optimal size relation is only cited.
Only MLPs with 3 hidden layers and varying width; no shape comparison at fixed size.
Only size scaling of AlphaZero playing strength is tested. Not tested: compute or data scaling, a fitted loss power law, other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
No comparison of LM fitting methods, parameter counting, schedules or compute-optimal splits.

missing.what: Connect Four Elo-versus-size scaling exponent as a function of inference temperature, and its nonlinear correlation with the Zipf tail exponent.
Pre-break steady size-scaling segment for Oware and Checkers, and the alternate-hyperparameter Oware suite reaching higher Elo.

record.verdict_notes: The inverse-scaling result is about Elo (playing strength), not loss. Connect Four and Pentago scaling laws come from the authors' earlier paper (Neumann & Gros 2022); the models are reused. The bending of the curve resembles V7's 'curves can bend', but V7 concerns LM law fitting, so it is linked to V5 here. No numeric exponents or break points are given in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or loss-versus-parameters/tokens/compute power-law measurement.
No fits to small runs or tests of predictions on much larger runs.
No compute-budget allocation sweep or optimal parameter/token split.
The paper does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests AlphaZero reinforcement learning only. It does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer, and does not fit a general loss power law over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No downstream language-model task evaluation or prediction from pretraining loss.
Does not compare parameter-counting conventions, fitting methods, training schedules, or compute-optimal splits; its inverse-scaling results concern AlphaZero size-scaling curves.

rows.subject: Checkers AlphaZero agents
rows.size_stated: Varying neural-network sizes; exact sizes not stated
rows.operation_detail: Measured Elo scaling with neural-network size.
rows.value: The scaling curve abruptly changes direction at larger sizes and scales negatively beyond a certain size.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 5A error bars are one standard deviation; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The paper states that Checkers shows inverse scaling; no fitted exponent or exact break point is given.
rows.check: Relinked from V7 to V5. V7 concerns fitting and setup choices behind published LM laws; this is a non-text RL regime. The measure is Bradley-Terry strength/Elo, not loss. The scaling curve is steady below the break and reverses only beyond a size threshold, so the state applies to large sizes.

rows.subject: Oware AlphaZero agents
rows.size_stated: Varying neural-network sizes; exact sizes not stated
rows.operation_detail: Measured Elo scaling with neural-network size.
rows.value: The scaling curve abruptly changes direction at larger sizes and scales negatively beyond a certain size; a suite trained with different hyperparameters extends to higher Elo scores.
rows.uncertainty: Figure 5A error bars are one standard deviation; numerical values not stated.
rows.note: The hyperparameter suite is used to argue the break is not simply a perfect-play ceiling; exact sizes and Elo values are not stated.
rows.check: Relinked from V7 to V5 for the same reasons as r8. The reversal applies to large sizes only. A different-hyperparameter suite reaching higher Elo is used to rule out a perfect-play ceiling.

tranche.reason: The explicit reversal of scaling at large sizes in Oware and Checkers challenges the generality of V5.

source_check.notes: Power laws apply to Bradley-Terry strength, with Elo proportional to its logarithm. The supplied text is the October 2025 revision; no numerical break sizes or fitted inverse-scaling exponents are stated.

statements.correction: Oware/Checkers: Elo decreases beyond a network-size threshold (Figure 5A; Section 8). Connect Four: larger agents have significantly better solver-annotated ground-truth value loss (Figure 4B; Section 7); loss stagnates at the largest sizes as agents approach optimal play (Section 7, footnote 3). Solver-annotated states come from agents' training datasets (Appendix E).
statements.problem: The Oware/Checkers reversal is correct. The text does not describe Connect Four value-head test loss as flat/non-monotone or explicitly non-power-law, and does not identify the solver-annotated states as OOD. Numbers about other studies are outside this check.
